subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Rheumatology and 22q11: DiGeorge, Systemic JIA, and SLE

steps.tx: Microdeletions of chromosome 22q11.2 disrupt embryonic development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and branchial arches. The resulting neurocristopathy known as **DiGeorge anomaly in neonates** presents with a classic clinical tetrad comprising congenital conotruncal cardiac malformations (interrupted aortic arch, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot), neonatal hypocalcaemic tetany from parathyroid hypoplasia, thymic hypoplasia causing T-cell deficiency, and cleft palate.
steps.say: DiGeorge syndrome arises from 22q11.2 microdeletions affecting the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. It features conotruncal heart defects, hypocalcemia, and thymic aplasia.

left.title: CATCH-22 Clinical Spectrum
points: Cardiac defects: truncus arteriosus, interrupted arch, TOF
Abnormal facies: hooded eyelids, low-set ears, micrognathia
Thymic hypoplasia: T-cell immunodeficiency
Cleft palate: submucous cleft or velopharyngeal insufficiency
Hypocalcaemia: parathyroid gland aplasia / hypoplasia

right.title: Diagnostic & Emergency Management
points: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for 22q11.2
Or chromosomal microarray for microdeletion
Intravenous calcium gluconate for neonatal tetany
Irradiate all blood products to prevent fatal GVHD

steps.tx: Persistent inflammatory arthritis of unknown etiology lasting longer than six weeks in children under sixteen years defines juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Categorized under the International League of Associations for Rheumatology (ILAR), **juvenile idiopathic arthritis subtypes** comprise oligoarthritis (affecting four or fewer joints, accounting for fifty percent), polyarthritis (five or more joints), systemic JIA, enthesitis-related arthritis, and psoriatic arthritis.
steps.say: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis requires persistent joint inflammation for at least six weeks in children under sixteen. Oligoarthritis is the most common subtype, affecting four or fewer joints.

steps.tx: Asymptomatic chronic non-granulomatous anterior uveitis threatens irreversible visual loss in young girls with oligoarticular arthritis. Characterized by high positivity for antinuclear antibodies, **chronic uveitis in oligoarticular JIA** develops insidiously without pain, redness, or photophobia. Regular routine slit-lamp biomicroscopy every three to four months is mandatory to detect anterior chamber inflammatory flare and cells before posterior synechiae, band keratopathy, or cataracts develop.
steps.say: Chronic anterior uveitis in oligoarticular JIA is completely silent and painless in ANA-positive toddlers. Regular slit-lamp exams detect cells before cataracts and blindness ensue.

left.title: Silent Uveitis Risk Profile
points: Young girls (onset <6 years of age)
Oligoarticular joint involvement pattern
Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) serology
Completely white, painless eye without symptoms

right.title: Slit-Lamp Surveillance Rules
points: Screening every 3 months for high-risk ANA-positive girls
Identifies anterior chamber cells and protein flare
Topical corticosteroid drops (prednisolone acetate)
Methotrexate or anti-TNF (adalimumab) for refractory uveitis

steps.tx: A distinctive autoinflammatory presentation driven by interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 cytokine cascades manifests with spiking fevers and systemic toxicity. Classically designated Still disease, **systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis** (sJIA) is characterized by quotidian spiking fevers touching baseline daily, an evanescent salmon-pink macular rash that peaks with the fever spike, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, serositis, and severe polyarthritis.
steps.say: Systemic JIA features daily quotidian spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, lymphadenopathy, and high inflammatory markers. It is driven by IL-1 and IL-6 cytokines.

vis.alt: Clinical and laboratory collage showing quotidian fever chart, salmon-pink evanescent rash, and polyarthritis in systemic JIA.
vis.caption: Diagnostic features of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis showing quotidian fever spikes and transient salmon rash. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Uncontrolled hyperactivation of T-lymphocytes and well-differentiated macrophages triggers life-threatening hemophagocytic cytokine storm in systemic arthritis. The most dangerous complication of sJIA is **macrophage activation syndrome** (MAS), presenting with persistent non-remitting fever, profound coagulopathy with falling fibrinogen, paradoxical drop in erythrocyte sedimentation rate from fibrinogen consumption, massive hyperferritinaemia, cytopenias, and hemophagocytosis on bone marrow biopsy.
steps.say: Macrophage activation syndrome is a fatal cytokine storm in systemic JIA. A sudden drop in ESR, paradoxical falling platelets, and ferritin in the thousands are classic signs.

rows: Sensitive biomarker for acute MAS onset
Consumption of plasma fibrinogen in DIC

steps.tx: Targeted biologic monoclonal antibodies neutralize specific cytokine mediators in refractory juvenile arthritis. While conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs like weekly subcutaneous methotrexate remain first-line for polyarthritis, **biologic therapies in juvenile arthritis** utilize interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, canakinumab) and interleukin-6 inhibitors (tocilizumab) to induce dramatic clinical remission in systemic JIA, and TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab) in polyarthritis.
steps.say: Interleukin-1 blockers like anakinra and interleukin-6 inhibitors like tocilizumab have revolutionized systemic JIA treatment. TNF blockers control polyarthritis.

left.title: Systemic JIA Biologics (IL-1 / IL-6)
points: Anakinra: recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist
Canakinumab: monoclonal anti-IL-1-beta antibody
Tocilizumab: monoclonal anti-IL-6 receptor antibody
Rapidly resolves fevers, rash, and arthritis

right.title: Polyarticular JIA Biologics (TNF-alpha)
points: Etanercept: recombinant TNF receptor fusion protein
Adalimumab: fully human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody
Methotrexate is co-administered to prevent antidrug antibodies
Annual screening for latent tuberculosis mandatory

steps.tx: Multisystem autoimmune disease driven by pathogenic antinuclear autoantibodies and immune complex deposition affects adolescent females. In **pediatric systemic lupus erythematosus** (pSLE), presenting features are more severe than in adults, frequently presenting with malar butterfly rash, photosensitivity, oral mucosal ulcers, non-erosive polyarthritis, serositis, and autoimmune cytopenias (Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia).
steps.say: Pediatric lupus is more aggressive than adult SLE, with higher rates of renal involvement. Classic features include a malar butterfly rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, and cytopenias.

rows: Best initial screening test for pSLE
Negative ANA virtually rules out lupus
Strong correlation with active lupus nephritis
Remains positive indefinitely; no flare tracking
Markedly depressed during active disease flares
Consumption via classical immune complex pathway

steps.tx: Renal involvement occurs in up to eighty percent of pediatric lupus patients, dictating long-term survival and morbidity. Evaluation of **pediatric lupus nephritis** requires routine screening with urinalysis for proteinuria, microscopic haematuria, and cellular red blood cell casts. Percutaneous core renal biopsy is mandatory to classify glomerular involvement from Class I (minimal mesangial) to Class IV (diffuse proliferative, the most severe), guiding mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide therapy.
steps.say: Lupus nephritis affects eighty percent of pediatric SLE patients. Core renal biopsy is mandatory to classify disease, with diffuse proliferative Class four requiring intense therapy.

left.title: ISN/RPS Nephritis Classification
points: Class I: Minimal mesangial lupus nephritis
Class II: Mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis
Class III: Focal proliferative lupus nephritis (<50% glomeruli)
Class IV: Diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (>50% glomeruli)
Class V: Membranous nephropathy; Class VI: Advanced sclerosis

right.title: Class IV Induction Chemotherapy
points: High-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone
Combined with oral mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)
Or intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus protocol)
Hydroxychloroquine is universally prescribed for all pSLE

steps.tx: Loops of wire under the microscope predict how hard lupus will hit the kidney. **Class IV lupus nephritis** shows diffuse proliferation with wire loop deposits thickening capillary walls, the pattern most likely to destroy renal function without aggressive immunosuppression. Biopsy class, not urine sediment alone, chooses that intensity. Children are biopsied readily because their disease is so often proliferative beneath a deceptively stable creatinine.
steps.say: Class IV lupus nephritis shows diffuse proliferation and wire loop capillary deposits. Biopsy class decides immunosuppression intensity in children.

vis.alt: Renal biopsy microscopy of class IV diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis with wire loop lesions.
vis.caption: Thickened wire loop capillary walls fill glomeruli in diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis. Illustration: StewardMD original.
